lessonTitle: Inborn Errors of Metabolism: Recognition and Screening

blocks.text: On the fifth day of life, a nurse pricks a newborn's heel and presses four drops of blood onto a filter-paper card. The baby looks perfectly healthy. Weeks later the result flags a disease that would have caused severe, irreversible brain damage, yet one that a special diet prevents almost completely. This is newborn screening, and it works only because we understand how a single missing enzyme alters biochemistry.

blocks.markdown: **The idea.** An **inborn error of metabolism (IEM)** is a genetic disease in which a mutation reduces the activity of an enzyme, transporter or cofactor-handling protein. Most are **autosomal recessive**: a child is affected only if both copies of the gene are defective, so both parents are usually healthy carriers. Each IEM is individually rare, but together they are an important cause of illness in infants and children.

blocks.title: Inborn error of metabolism
blocks.text: A genetically determined block in a metabolic pathway, usually an enzyme deficiency. The block causes accumulation of the substrate (and of metabolites formed by alternative routes), a deficiency of the product, or both.

blocks.markdown: **Consequences of an enzyme block.** Consider a pathway A to B to C to D, with the enzyme converting B to C deficient. Three things follow: (1) **substrate accumulation**: B (and A behind it) builds up, and may be toxic; (2) **product deficiency**: C and D fall, so anything depending on them is lacking; (3) **alternative pathways**: the accumulated B is diverted to side-products that are normally minor and may be toxic or useful as diagnostic markers. Which of the three dominates tells you the clinical picture, and it also tells you the treatment: restrict the substrate, supply the missing product, or remove the toxic metabolite.

blocks.title: Predicting the biochemistry of a block
blocks.prompt: In a pathway W to X to Y to Z, the enzyme that converts X to Y is absent. Predict plasma levels and a possible treatment strategy.

steps.text: Substrate side: X accumulates and W also rises behind the block.
Product side: Y and Z fall, since the only route to them is blocked.
Alternative route: accumulated X may be converted to a side-product X', which appears in blood or urine and can serve as a diagnostic marker.
Treatment follows from the three effects: limit dietary W or X, supplement Y or Z, and clear X' if it is toxic.

blocks.answer: X and W high, Y and Z low, with an abnormal side-product X'. Treat by restricting substrate and replacing product.

blocks.markdown: **Phenylketonuria (PKU).** In PKU, the liver enzyme **phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH)** is deficient (or, in a minority, its cofactor **tetrahydrobiopterin, BH4**, is deficient). PAH normally converts the essential amino acid phenylalanine to **tyrosine**. When blocked: **phenylalanine accumulates** in blood and brain (the substrate effect) and is toxic to the developing brain; **tyrosine becomes an essential amino acid** (the product effect), with reduced melanin (fair skin and hair) and reduced catecholamine synthesis; and phenylalanine is diverted to **phenylketones** (phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate), producing a mousy or musty odour. The infant is normal at birth because maternal metabolism protects the fetus; damage accumulates as protein feeding begins. Untreated PKU causes intellectual disability, seizures and behavioural problems.

blocks.title: Why newborn screening is justified
blocks.text: A disease is suitable for screening when it is (1) serious, (2) present but silent at birth, (3) detectable by a cheap, reliable test, and (4) treatable so that early treatment prevents harm. PKU meets all four: a drop of blood taken after feeding is established (typically within the first week; timing varies by programme) detects raised phenylalanine, and lifelong dietary phenylalanine restriction started early largely prevents brain damage. Women with PKU who are pregnant must keep phenylalanine low, because high maternal phenylalanine crosses the placenta and harms the fetus (microcephaly, heart defects, learning difficulty), even when the fetus does not itself have PKU.

rows: Normal at birth; developmental delay, seizures, fair skin, musty odour; raised blood phenylalanine
Vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, cataracts after milk feeds; infection risk; urine reducing substance positive
Leucine, isoleucine, valine and their keto acids
Poor feeding, lethargy, seizures in first days; urine smelling of maple syrup or burnt sugar
blocks.caption: A few well-known inborn errors and their recognisable clues.

blocks.title: How good is a screening test for a rare disease?
blocks.prompt: A programme screens 20,000 newborns for a disorder with prevalence 1 in 10,000. The test detects every true case but gives a false positive in 0.5% of unaffected babies. What fraction of positive screens are true cases (positive predictive value)?

steps.text: True cases = 20,000 x (1/10,000) = 2. All are detected, so 2 true positives.
Unaffected babies = 20,000 - 2 = 19,998. False positives = 0.5% of 19,998, about 100.

blocks.answer: About 2%. Most positive screens in a rare disease are false alarms, so a positive screen leads to a confirmatory test rather than a diagnosis.

blocks.markdown: **Recognising an IEM clinically.** Suspect an IEM in an infant or child who has: poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, seizures or coma after a period of normality (often after protein or milk introduction, or during fasting or intercurrent illness); an unexplained metabolic acidosis, hypoglycaemia or hyperammonaemia; unusual body odour; failure to thrive, hepatomegaly, cataracts or developmental regression; parental consanguinity or an unexplained sibling death. Laboratory clues include a high anion gap acidosis, raised lactate, raised ammonia, hypoglycaemia with or without ketones, and urine reducing substances.

items: First-line tests in an acutely unwell infant: blood glucose, blood gas with anion gap, lactate, ammonia, ketones.
Specialist tests: plasma amino acids, urine organic acids and acylcarnitine profile (tandem mass spectrometry).
Confirmation: enzyme assay or DNA analysis of the gene.
Management always starts with stopping the offending intake, supporting glucose and removing toxic compounds.

blocks.title: Substrate up, product down
blocks.text: For any IEM question, write the pathway on paper, mark the block, then list what rises (substrate and side-products) and what falls (product). Features usually follow from one of these two lists.

points: An inborn error of metabolism is a genetic enzyme or transporter defect, usually autosomal recessive, causing substrate accumulation, product deficiency and alternative-pathway metabolites.
In PKU, phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency raises phenylalanine and makes tyrosine essential; early dietary restriction prevents brain damage.
Newborn screening suits diseases that are serious, silent at birth, testable and treatable, but positive predictive value for rare diseases is low so positives need confirming.
Clues to an IEM include collapse after feeds, acidosis, hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia, unusual odour, consanguinity and family history.

questions.stem: Classical phenylketonuria is caused by deficiency of which enzyme?

options.text: Phenylalanine hydroxylase
Tyrosinase
Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase
Branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase

distractorRationale.a: Correct: PAH converts phenylalanine to tyrosine, and its deficiency causes PKU.
distractorRationale.b: Tyrosinase is needed for melanin synthesis; its absence causes albinism, not PKU.
distractorRationale.c: This enzyme is deficient in classical galactosaemia.
distractorRationale.d: This enzyme is deficient in maple syrup urine disease.

questions.explanation: Phenylalanine hydroxylase hydroxylates phenylalanine to tyrosine in the liver. Without it phenylalanine accumulates, which is the biochemical basis of phenylketonuria.

questions.stem: Why do patients with untreated phenylketonuria tend to have fair skin and hair?

options.text: Tyrosine, the precursor of melanin, is deficient because it cannot be made from phenylalanine
Tyrosinase is mutated in all patients
Phenylketones bleach melanocytes
Phenylalanine is converted into a melanin inhibitor in the skin

questions.correctOptionText: Tyrosine, the precursor of melanin, is deficient because it cannot be made from phenylalanine

distractorRationale.a: Correct: product deficiency: lack of tyrosine limits melanin (and catecholamine) synthesis.
distractorRationale.b: Tyrosinase mutations cause albinism; in PKU tyrosinase is normal but short of substrate.
distractorRationale.c: There is no evidence that phenylketones bleach melanocytes; the effect is substrate-limited synthesis.
distractorRationale.d: No such inhibitor is formed; the explanation is a product deficiency.

questions.explanation: PAH normally supplies tyrosine, which is the precursor of melanin and the catecholamines. When PAH is deficient, tyrosine becomes an essential amino acid and pigment synthesis falls, illustrating the product-deficiency effect of an enzyme block.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why phenylketonuria is suitable for population newborn screening?

options.text: Affected infants look normal at birth, damage is preventable, and early dietary treatment is effective
It is the most common cause of neonatal death
The disease cannot be diagnosed after infancy
The screening test has a positive predictive value of 100%

questions.correctOptionText: Affected infants look normal at birth, damage is preventable, and early dietary treatment is effective

distractorRationale.a: Correct: serious, silent at birth, detectable and treatable are the criteria that justify screening.
distractorRationale.b: PKU is not a leading cause of neonatal death; its harm is progressive brain injury.
distractorRationale.c: PKU can be diagnosed at any age; the benefit of screening is early treatment.
distractorRationale.d: Screening tests for rare conditions generate many false positives, so predictive value is not 100%.

questions.explanation: Screening is justified when a disease is serious but presymptomatic at birth and early treatment changes the outcome. PKU fits: phenylalanine restriction begun in the first weeks largely prevents intellectual disability.

questions.stem: A 4-day-old full-term infant, previously feeding well, becomes lethargic with vomiting and poor feeding and has a high-pitched cry. The nurse notes that the urine smells of burnt sugar or maple syrup. Which metabolic defect is most likely?

options.text: Defective breakdown of the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine and valine
Defective conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine
Defective conversion of galactose-1-phosphate to glucose-1-phosphate
Defective glycogen phosphorylase in muscle

questions.correctOptionText: Defective breakdown of the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine and valine

distractorRationale.a: Correct: maple syrup urine disease is caused by branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency, with the characteristic odour.
distractorRationale.b: PKU is usually silent in the first days and has a mousy odour rather than a maple syrup smell.
distractorRationale.c: Galactosaemia causes jaundice, hepatomegaly and cataracts, and does not give a maple syrup odour.
distractorRationale.d: Muscle phosphorylase deficiency presents with exercise cramps, not neonatal encephalopathy.

questions.explanation: A previously well neonate who deteriorates after protein feeds and has urine with a maple syrup odour has maple syrup urine disease. Accumulating branched-chain amino acids and their keto acids are neurotoxic.

questions.stem: A woman with phenylketonuria stops her low-phenylalanine diet and then becomes pregnant. Her partner is not a carrier. Why is her fetus at risk?

options.text: High maternal phenylalanine crosses the placenta and damages the developing fetus, even if the fetus does not have PKU
The fetus will certainly inherit PKU and be born with symptoms
Maternal tyrosine excess is toxic to fetal liver
The fetus cannot receive any amino acids across the placenta

questions.correctOptionText: High maternal phenylalanine crosses the placenta and damages the developing fetus, even if the fetus does not have PKU

distractorRationale.a: Correct: maternal hyperphenylalaninaemia is teratogenic (microcephaly, cardiac defects, learning difficulty).
distractorRationale.b: The fetus will be an obligate carrier, not affected, since the father is not a carrier.
distractorRationale.c: Tyrosine is deficient, not in excess, in PKU.
distractorRationale.d: Amino acids are actively transported across the placenta; that is how phenylalanine reaches the fetus.

questions.explanation: The fetus is a carrier only, but it is exposed to the high phenylalanine in the maternal blood. Maternal PKU therefore causes fetal harm unless diet control is re-established before conception.

questions.stem: True or false: an infant with untreated classical phenylketonuria usually appears normal at birth.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Maternal metabolism protects the fetus, so the baby is normal at birth. Damage develops after protein feeding starts, which is why screening and early diet matter.

questions.stem: Two healthy parents have a first child with an autosomal recessive inborn error. Their second child is healthy. What is the probability, as a percentage, that this healthy second child is a carrier?
questions.explanation: Both parents must be carriers (Aa x Aa), so offspring are 25% AA, 50% Aa and 25% aa. Excluding the affected genotype aa, the healthy child is Aa with probability 50 / 75 = 2/3, which is 66.7 percent.

questions.stem: A screening programme tests 100,000 newborns for a disorder of prevalence 1 in 20,000. The test detects every affected baby and has a false positive rate of 0.1% in unaffected babies; treat the number of unaffected babies as 100,000. What is the positive predictive value, as a percentage?
questions.explanation: True cases = 100,000 / 20,000 = 5, all detected. False positives = 0.1% of 100,000 = 100. Positive predictive value = 5 / (5 + 100) = 0.048, or about 4.8 percent, so most positives are false alarms and need confirmatory testing.

questions.stem: Using phenylketonuria as an example, explain how an enzyme deficiency leads to substrate accumulation, product deficiency and the formation of alternative metabolites, and relate each to a clinical feature.
markingGuide: Phenylalanine hydroxylase converts phenylalanine to tyrosine; the enzyme is deficient
Substrate accumulation: raised phenylalanine, toxic to developing brain, causing intellectual disability and seizures
Product deficiency: tyrosine becomes essential; reduced melanin (fair skin and hair) and reduced catecholamines
Alternative pathway: phenylalanine converted to phenylketones (phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate), excreted in urine and giving a musty odour
Treatment follows: restrict dietary phenylalanine and supply tyrosine
questions.explanation: A block at one enzyme produces predictable consequences upstream and downstream, as well as diversion into side pathways. PKU shows all three effects and each gives a recognisable clinical or laboratory feature.

questions.stem: A 3-day-old infant becomes lethargic and starts vomiting after feeds. List the clinical and laboratory clues that would make you suspect an inborn error of metabolism, and name the first-line and specialist investigations you would request.
markingGuide: Clinical clues: deterioration after a period of normality, poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, seizures, unusual odour, hepatomegaly, jaundice, cataracts, failure to thrive
History clues: parental consanguinity, unexplained sibling death or family history
Laboratory clues: metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap, raised lactate, hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia, urine reducing substances
First-line tests: glucose, blood gas and anion gap, lactate, ammonia, ketones
Specialist tests: plasma amino acids, urine organic acids, acylcarnitine profile by tandem mass spectrometry
Confirmation by enzyme assay or DNA analysis
questions.explanation: Inborn errors present with nonspecific signs that mimic sepsis, so the pattern of acidosis, ammonia and glucose together with a family history directs the investigation. First-line tests are rapid and guide emergency treatment, while specialist tests identify the specific defect.
